lines: Git showed you exit codes. This refresher is where they come from.
Five minutes on processes, signals and pipes: the machinery under every command you type and every job you schedule.
All familiar? Swipe on to the delivery workflow.
Every program you run is three steps. Follow the three arrows.
The shell forks a copy of itself. The copy replaces itself with the program you asked for. And the shell waits.
What comes back is a single number, the exit status. That is the number Git's bisect read, and the one every script checks.
And notice what the child inherits: three open files, numbered zero, one and two, for input, output and errors. Everything about redirection is moving those numbers.
Permissions are nine bits: read, write and execute for the owner, the group, and everyone else.
A new file usually starts with read and write for all three, and the umask switches bits off. The nightly job writes its file under a strict umask.
The loader, another user in the same group, opens the file. Can it read it?
answer: That umask switches off every bit for the group and for others, so the file ends up readable and writable by its owner alone.
The common wrong guess is that a group member can read a new file, because that is the default on many systems. The mask is exactly what changes it.

lines: Redirections are applied strictly left to right. That detail causes one of the most common mistakes in shell scripts.
The redirect that copies stream two onto stream one means: make two point wherever one points right now.
So look at the order in the command. At the moment of the copy, stream one is still the terminal.
The job prints one error line. Where does it land?
answer: Stream two was copied while stream one still pointed at the terminal. Only afterwards was stream one moved to the file, and the copy did not follow it.
So the log file stays empty. Write the file redirect first and the copy second, and the error lands in the file.

lines: A pipe feeds one command's output into the next one's input. Now ask: what is the status of the whole line?
It is the status of the last command, and only that. Hold on to this, because it hides failures.
A command at the front can't open its file. The later ones are quite happy to process nothing.
What does the shell report?
answer: The last command succeeded, so the line did, and the failure at the front was invisible. That is how a broken nightly job exits cleanly.
The pipefail option makes the status the last failure instead. Put it with the strict options at the top of the script, and the job stops right there instead of carrying on with an empty result.

lines: An exit status is one byte, so it lives between zero and two hundred and fifty five. Zero is success.
The shell adds two codes of its own: one for found but not executable, one for command not found.
And above one hundred and twenty eight, the convention is a hundred and twenty eight plus the signal that killed the program.
So a hundred and thirty seven is a kill, a hundred and forty three is a terminate request, and a hundred and thirty is Ctrl and C. It is a convention: a program could return those numbers itself.
A signal is a message that is one number long. Two matter most.
Terminate is the polite one. The job catches it, flushes its buffers, closes its files, and re raises it, so the shell sees the terminate code.
Kill cannot be caught or ignored. The kernel removes the process where it stands, so buffers are lost, and the shell sees the kill code.
That asymmetry is why you ask first and only force it after a grace period. And a child nobody waited for lingers as a zombie.
A scenario you will meet. The nightly load has made no progress for an hour. The kernel's live view of the process says sleeping, with two threads.
Then you attach a tracer to see its system calls. It shows a read on one file descriptor, and nothing after it.
What is it doing?
answer: Waiting inside a read, on a socket nobody is writing to.
A sleeping state is not a busy loop, which would show the processor in use. And a disk wait would show a different state. A zombie has no open calls at all.
So the load is blocked on its own input, and a timeout on that read is the real fix.

lines: Now put the pieces together. One pipeline pulls a field from each line, trims and lowercases it, then sorts and counts.
The same job in a script gives the same answer, and comparing the two prints nothing and exits zero.
Skip the cleaning step and stray capitals and blanks make extra groups. A plain search for one word misses the padded variant.
So count values after parsing them, not strings. The deep dive has the script and every way it breaks.
Two last tools. A scheduled job has five time fields and then the command. This one runs at the same time every night and appends both streams to a log.
Scheduled jobs get a tiny environment, nothing from your shell, run in one timezone, and nothing stops a second copy starting while the first still runs. So take a lock.
On the nights clocks change, a local time can be missing or happen twice, so run the scheduler in universal time.
And to reach a database behind a bastion, forward a local port through it.
Nine things to keep. Fork, exec, wait. Permissions and the mask. Redirections apply left to right.
A pipeline reports its last command unless you ask otherwise. Exit codes are one byte. Terminate asks and kill does not.
Read a hung process from its state and its system calls. And a scheduled job needs a lock and a clock you control.
